Samarkand, the capital of the Silk Road: a jewel of Central Asia that captivates hearts

Uzbekistan, an enchanting land in the heart of Central Asia, is a living testimony to the greatness of ancient civilisations and the splendour of the Silk Road, which linked East and West for many centuries. It is a unique destination, rich in history, culture and stunning natural scenery, that attracts travellers looking for an exceptional and profound experience. From its vast deserts to its towering mountain peaks, and from ancient cities that tell countless stories to bustling markets teeming with life, Uzbekistan offers visitors a journey through time into a world of legends and magnificent architecture.

Uzbekistan’s strategic location has long made it a meeting point of civilisations and a thriving centre of trade and culture. Uzbek cities such as Samarkand, Bukhara and Khiva were for centuries beacons of science, learning and art, where Islamic scholarship, astronomy, medicine and philosophy flourished. Islamic architecture is the dominant feature of these cities, with their ancient mosques, religious schools (madrasas) and grand mausoleums decorated with brightly coloured tiles and intricate geometric patterns: timeless masterpieces that reflect the genius of the designers and craftsmen of that golden age.

Visiting Uzbekistan is an invitation to immerse yourself in a rich cultural tapestry, where authentic Uzbek hospitality, deep-rooted customs and traditions, and delicious cuisine are an integral part of the experience. Travellers find themselves surrounded by historical tales, folk legends and a warm welcome from locals who are keen to share their heritage with visitors. It is a journey that promises many discoveries, whether historical, cultural or personal, and leaves a deep impression on everyone who sets foot in this captivating country, which still keeps the spirit of the Silk Road alive in every corner.

Top places to visit: architectural masterpieces that tell a story

Uzbekistan is full of priceless architectural and historical treasures, each a chapter in the story of the Great Silk Road. Visiting these places is not just about seeing ancient buildings; it is a deep dive into the spirit of the Islamic and Persian civilisation that flourished in this region.

Samarkand: the pearl of the East that still shines

Samarkand is undoubtedly the beating heart of Uzbekistan and one of the most important cities on the Silk Road. The mere mention of its name conjures images of grandeur and a rich history. It is a legendary city that was once the capital of great empires and a centre of science and art. Registan Square, whose name translates as “sandy square”, is a unique architectural masterpiece and the symbol of Samarkand. The square is framed by three stately madrasas, known together as the “Triple Madrasa”: the Ulugh Beg Madrasa, the Sher-Dor Madrasa and the Tilya-Kori Madrasa. They have exquisite façades of turquoise and dark blue tiles, with intricate geometric patterns and delicate floral decoration, reflecting the heyday of architecture in Central Asia.

  • Bibi-Khanym Mosque: This mosque, said to have been built by Timur for his beloved wife, was considered one of the largest and grandest mosques in the Islamic world of its time. Although time has left its mark, it still amazes visitors with its massive scale and towering turquoise domes.
  • Gur-e-Amir Mausoleum: This is the mausoleum of Emperor Timur (Tamerlane) and his descendants, and another architectural masterpiece, distinguished by its ribbed turquoise dome and elaborate interior of marble, gold and mosaics.
  • Shah-i-Zinda Avenue: Known as the “Cemetery of the Living King”, this avenue is a necropolis of mausoleums and tombs of members of the royal family and religious leaders, some dating back to the ninth century AD. It is an exceptionally beautiful and sacred place, where the colours of the tiles sparkle on every side like a mosaic of dreams.
  • Ulugh Beg Observatory: Ulugh Beg, Timur’s grandson, was a great astronomer who built an advanced observatory in the 15th century, considered one of the most important in history. Although only part of it still stands, it offers a glimpse of the scientific progress Samarkand saw in that era.
  • Siab Bazaar: This old market, near the Bibi-Khanym Mosque, is an ideal place to experience vibrant local life. Visitors can find aromatic spices, dried fruit, traditional Uzbek bread and handicrafts, and soak up the lively, bustling atmosphere.

Bukhara: the city of a thousand domes and a beacon of knowledge

Bukhara is no less important than Samarkand and is an open-air museum in itself, having kept its authentic character as if untouched by the passage of time. Its narrow streets, old mud-brick buildings and covered markets all take the visitor back to bygone eras.

  • Po-i-Kalon Ensemble: Bukhara’s skyline is dominated by the towering Kalon Minaret, also known as the “Tower of Death” because it was used in the past to execute criminals. The minaret is part of an architectural ensemble that includes the Kalon Mosque and the Mir-i-Arab Madrasa.
  • Lyabi-Hauz: This peaceful square, with a large pool surrounded by ancient trees and historic buildings such as the Nadir Divan-Begi Madrasa and the Nadir Divan-Begi Khanqah, is an ideal place to relax and enjoy the tranquil atmosphere.
  • Chor Minor Madrasa: Its name means “four minarets”. It is a unique madrasa with four small minarets topped by turquoise domes, creating a distinctive architectural sight.
  • Samanid Mausoleum: This mausoleum, which dates back to the ninth or tenth century AD, is one of the oldest examples of Islamic architecture in Central Asia, and is known for its beautiful baked-brick design, which changes colour with the sunlight.

Khiva: a city of legends and fairy tales

Khiva is a city surrounded by high mud-brick walls, as if it had come straight out of the pages of a fairy tale. Itchan Kala, the walled inner city, is a UNESCO World Heritage Site with more than 50 historical monuments and 250 old houses, all exquisitely preserved.

  • Kunya Ark Citadel: The old citadel was the residence of the rulers of Khiva and includes several buildings such as the Summer Mosque, the Throne Room and the prison. It offers wonderful panoramic views of the city.
  • Kalta Minor Minaret: Covered all over in bright blue and green tiles, this “short” minaret, which was never completed, is a distinctive symbol of Khiva.
  • Tash-Hauli Palace: This palace, built by Allakuli Khan, is considered one of the most beautiful in Khiva. It has more than 150 rooms and inner courtyards decorated with beautiful tiles, and reflects the luxury of life at the royal court.
  • Juma (Friday) Mosque: This mosque is unique, with 213 finely carved wooden columns and an atmosphere of tranquillity and solemnity.

Tashkent: a modern capital with deep roots

Tashkent, the capital of Uzbekistan, is a large, modern city that still retains its historical and cultural treasures. It is a unique combination of tall Soviet-era buildings, spacious green parks and old neighbourhoods that tell stories of a bygone past.

  • Hazrati Imam Complex: This religious complex is an important Islamic centre and includes the Barak-Khan Madrasa, the Tilla Sheikh Mosque and the mausoleum of Abu Bakr al-Qaffal al-Shashi, as well as the Muyi Muborak Library. The Uthman Quran, one of the oldest copies of the Holy Quran in the world, is now displayed in the Centre of Islamic Civilisation next door.
  • Amir Temur Square: This square is the centre of modern Tashkent, with a huge statue of Amir Temur on horseback surrounded by modern and historic buildings.
  • Chorsu Bazaar: This large blue-domed market is one of the largest and oldest markets in Tashkent, and a great place to experience the bustling local atmosphere and buy fresh produce, spices and handicrafts.

Fergana Valley: the cradle of handicrafts and natural beauty

The Fergana Valley is known for its fertility and natural beauty, and as a centre of traditional Uzbek crafts such as silk-making, pottery and ceramics. The valley offers a different experience away from the historic cities, focusing on rural life and local arts.

Best time to visit: enjoy the beauty of the seasons

Choosing the right time to visit Uzbekistan can make a big difference to the quality of your experience. Uzbekistan has a continental climate, with very hot summers and cold winters, so the best times to visit are spring and autumn, when the weather is mild and ideal for exploring.

  • Spring (April - May): This is an ideal time: the weather is pleasant and sunny, and temperatures are mild and well suited to walking and touring the ancient cities. Flowers are in bloom, the landscape is green, and many local festivals are held, such as Nowruz (Persian New Year) in March, adding an atmosphere of joy and celebration.
  • Autumn (September - October): This is another golden season for travel, when the weather is cool and crisp and the trees display beautiful autumn colours. It is an ideal time to enjoy the historical sites without the intense heat of summer or the bitter cold of winter. It is also harvest time, which means an abundance of fresh fruit and vegetables in the markets.
  • Summer (June - August): Summer can be very hot, especially in July and August, when temperatures soar. If you choose to travel at this time, it is best to focus on indoor activities and museum visits, and to sightsee in the early morning or evening.
  • Winter (November - March): Winter can be very cold, with snow in some areas. Although some sites may be less crowded, the cold can make wandering outdoors less enjoyable. However, winter offers the unique beauty of snow-covered landscapes, and prices are often lower in this season.

So, for a comfortable and enjoyable trip, we highly recommend visiting Uzbekistan in spring or autumn to enjoy everything this wonderful Silk Road country has to offer.

Budget and costs: an affordable journey through history

Uzbekistan is a budget-friendly destination compared with many other countries, allowing travellers to enjoy a rich experience without spending a fortune. The country offers a variety of accommodation, transport, food and entertainment options to suit different budgets.

  • Accommodation: Accommodation ranges from charming traditional guesthouses in ancient cities like Bukhara and Khiva, which offer an authentic experience at very reasonable prices, to modern, full-service hotels in major cities like Tashkent and Samarkand. You can find rooms from $20-30 in clean, comfortable guesthouses, up to $100 or more in luxury hotels.
  • Food: Food in Uzbekistan is delicious, hearty and, most importantly, very affordable. Local restaurants serve generous traditional meals such as plov (a rice dish with meat and vegetables), shashlik (grilled meat), samsa (filled pastries) and manti (steamed dumplings) for just a few dollars per meal. Even in the most upmarket restaurants, an average meal will cost no more than $10-15.
  • Transport: Uzbekistan offers efficient and economical transport options.
    • High-speed trains (Afrosiyob): Modern high-speed trains connect major cities such as Tashkent, Samarkand, and Bukhara, and are the most comfortable and efficient way to travel between these cities. Ticket prices are very reasonable.
    • Regular trains: They offer a more economical option for travelling longer distances or to other cities such as Khiva.
    • Taxis: Taxis are a cheap and readily available way to get around within cities. It is best to agree the price before you set off.
    • Buses: Buses are the cheapest means of transport, but may be slower and less comfortable.
  • Entry fees: Entrance fees to historical sites and museums are generally nominal and will not put much strain on your budget.
  • Shopping and souvenirs: Uzbek markets and bazaars offer a wide range of handicrafts, textiles, ceramics and wooden items at reasonable prices, and you can bargain in most of them.

In general, a mid-range traveller can enjoy an excellent trip to Uzbekistan on $50-80 per day, including accommodation, food, local transport and entrance fees. If you’re looking for a little more luxury, costs will rise, but will still be much lower than in other tourist destinations.

Tips for Arab travellers: a comfortable and rewarding trip

For Arab travellers, Uzbekistan offers a unique and hospitable experience, with much shared culture and religion that makes a visit comfortable and enjoyable. Here are some tips for a smooth and rewarding trip:

  • Cultural and religious respect:
    • Uzbekistan is a Muslim-majority country, so it is advisable to dress modestly, especially when visiting mosques, shrines and madrasas. It is best to cover the shoulders and knees, and women are advised to carry a scarf to cover their heads when entering holy places.
    • Greeting locals with “As-salamu alaykum” (peace be upon you) is met with a smile and great appreciation.
  • Language and communication:
    • The official language is Uzbek, and Russian is widely spoken. In big cities and tourist areas you will find people who speak English, especially in tourist hotels and restaurants.
    • It is a good idea to download a translation app on your phone or carry a phrasebook to help with everyday communication. Learning a few basic words like “thank you” (rahmat) and “hello” (salaam) makes it easier to interact with locals.
  • Halal food:
    • As this is a Muslim-majority country, most of the food served is halal. You won’t have any trouble finding halal meat, and many restaurants have alcohol-free menus.
    • Take the opportunity to try local specialities such as plov, shashlik, samsa and shurpa, which are an integral part of Uzbek culture.
  • Currency and money:
    • The local currency is the Uzbek som (UZS). Major foreign currencies (such as US dollars and euros) can easily be exchanged at banks and authorised exchange offices.
    • It is advisable to carry some small notes for use in local markets and for short journeys, as some small establishments may not accept credit cards.
  • Safety and security:
    • Uzbekistan is generally considered a safe country for travellers. However, it is wise to take the usual precautions, such as keeping an eye on your personal belongings in crowded places.
    • If using taxis, it is best to agree the price before setting off to avoid misunderstandings.
  • Communications and internet:
    • Buying a local SIM card on arrival is easy and affordable, and gives you internet access and the ability to make calls. Local mobile operators offer good data packages.
    • Wi-Fi is available in most large tourist hotels and restaurants.
  • Bargaining in the markets:
    • Bargaining is a normal part of the shopping experience in Uzbek bazaars and markets. Feel free to haggle over prices, especially when buying souvenirs or handicrafts.
  • Water:
    • It is recommended to drink only bottled water and avoid tap water.
  • Uzbek hospitality:
    • The Uzbek people are known for their hospitality and warmth. Don’t be surprised if someone invites you for tea or a chat. Enjoy these moments, which offer an authentic glimpse of the local culture.

By following these tips, your trip to Uzbekistan will be an unforgettable experience, full of cultural and historical discoveries, and you will bring back priceless memories from the heart of the Silk Road.
